newsitem.title: FRANCE: Juppe's fate in forefront of French election.
newsitem.headline: Juppe's fate in forefront of French election.

text.p: The future of Prime Minister Alain Juppe has jumped to the forefront of France's election campaign amid mounting suggestions that he should go even if he leads the conservatives to victory.

Seen in opinion polls as one of the most unpopular French premiers on record, largely because of budget austerity and continuing record unemployment, Juppe is under attack from both opponents and some of his friends jockeying for power.

His left-wing foes, in a bid to frighten voters into ousting the centre-right, warn that Juppe could be in power until the term of President Jacques Chirac ends in five years, with a free hand to impose more austerity.
Some of his own allies have attacked Juppe for lacklustre campaigning and see him as an election liability although the latest opinion polls forecast a comfortable centre-right win.

Centrist former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, recalling that he had changed prime ministers during his 1974-81 term, has twice in a week suggested that President Jacques Chirac should form a new team even if Juppe's government won the May 25-June 1 vote.
"The people's idea is to retain the (centre-right) coalition but get a new way of governing," he told France 2 television on Tuesday night.
"The French people are disappointed. It would be imprudent not to heed their message ahead of a five-year period without any vote," he said.
Centrist former justice minister Pierre Mehaignerie openly discussed the choice of a new prime minister in a radio interview on Tuesday, saying that it should be a man mindful of the most humble.
Critics depict Juppe as a humourless, insensitive and authoritarian technocrat.
Opponents have dismissed suggestions that Chirac could fire an election-winning Juppe as a ploy to deceive voters.
Juppe has deflected questions about his own future, saying the election was about choosing a parliamentary majority rather than a prime minister.

But he has indicated that if he had to choose between the premiership and his job as mayor of Bordeaux under a proposed plan to ban politicians from holding two executive jobs, he would prefer to stay in Bordeaux.
Opinion polls regularly ask voters about their favourites for prime minister -- and consistently put Juppe way down the list.
The latest CSA survey released on Tuesday said the voters' top choice if the centre-right was returned to power was ex-National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin, a former anti-Maastricht campaigner.
Fellow-Gaullist ex-premier Edouard Balladur, Chirac's defeated rival for the presidency, came second ahead of ultra-liberal ex-finance minister Alain Madelin.
Another survey, by polling institute BVA, said most voters wanted Chirac to replace Juppe by someone from the private sector rather than by a professional politician.
Fifty-three percent suggested someone unconnected with the state to 24 percent who favoured a prime minister taken from Chirac's Gaullist RPR or its UDF centrist junior coalition partner.
